description: Search cars by coordinate, map rectangle, pick-up location or whole market, with the full filter and sort surface.

parameters.name: latitude
parameters.description:
**Latitude of the point to search around** (decimal degrees, WGS84).

Must be sent together with `longitude`. Examples: `34.0522` (Los Angeles), `40.7128` (New
York), `51.5074` (London, with `country=GB`), `43.6532` (Toronto, with `country=CA`).

Turo picks the radius itself from the density of cars around the point and echoes it back as
`searchLocation.appliedRadius`  -  about 34 miles around downtown Los Angeles. There is no
radius parameter to override it; use the bounding box when you need to control the area.

Range `-90` to `90`.

**Pick exactly ONE of the four ways to say where.** Mixing two returns a `400` naming the
conflict rather than quietly picking one for you:

- **A point**  -  `latitude` + `longitude`. Searches outward from a coordinate; each result carries
  its own `location.distance` back from that point, and the response echoes the radius Turo chose
  (`searchLocation.appliedRadius`, ~34 miles for a Los Angeles city centre point)
- **A bounding box**  -  `bottomLeftLatitude` + `bottomLeftLongitude` + `topRightLatitude` +
  `topRightLongitude`. Searches a rectangle, which is the right shape for a map viewport and the
  only way to tile a big market into pieces that each fit inside the 200-car response
- **A Turo pick-up location**  -  `locationId`, the numeric id of an airport or point of interest
  (`7894482` is LAX). Get one from `/location-details`, and use `pickupType` with it to say
  whether you want cars handed over AT that location or merely near it
- **A whole market**  -  `country` on its own, nothing else. Useful for "how much inventory is
  there in this country" (`totalHits`) rather than for browsing

`country` is required in all four modes  -  it selects the market, its currency and its catalogue.
Send half a pair (a `latitude` with no `longitude`, or three of the four box corners) and you get
a `400` naming the missing half rather than a silently different search.

parameters.name: bottomLeftLatitude
parameters.description:
**South edge of the search rectangle** (decimal degrees). Part of the bounding-box mode.

All four corners  -  `bottomLeftLatitude`, `bottomLeftLongitude`, `topRightLatitude`,
`topRightLongitude`  -  must be sent together; three of the four is a `400`.

A worked box around Los Angeles: `bottomLeftLatitude=33.90`, `bottomLeftLongitude=-118.45`,
`topRightLatitude=34.20`, `topRightLongitude=-118.10`.

**This is the mode to reach for when a market is bigger than one response.** Because a search
returns at most 200 cars, the way to enumerate a city is to cut it into tiles and search each
one: quarter the box, check `totalHits` on each quarter, and quarter again wherever it is
still above 200. The tiles do not overlap, so the results add up cleanly.

conflict rather than quietly picking one for you:

parameters.name: locationId
parameters.description:
**Numeric id of a Turo pick-up location**  -  an airport or a point of interest Turo hands
cars over at. This is the airport-rental mode.

Example: `7894482` is Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Ids come from
`/location-details`, which turns a place suggestion from `/location-autocomplete` into a
Turo location record carrying `locationId`, its coordinates and its
`availablePickupTypes`.

**Why use it instead of the airport's coordinates:** a `locationId` search is the airport
inventory as Turo itself defines it  -  the cars whose hosts have agreed to meet guests at that
terminal  -  rather than "every car within a radius of the runway". Pair it with `pickupType`
to choose between the two.

parameters.name: country
parameters.description:
**Market  -  a 2-letter ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 country code.** Case-insensitive.

Five markets carry inventory: `US`, `CA`, `GB`, `AU`, `FR`. Prices come back in that market's
currency (`USD`, `CAD`, `GBP`, `AUD`, `EUR`) and the make/model catalogue differs per market  - 
`/vehicle-makes` returns 65 makes for `US` and 45 for `CA`.

Any other valid code is accepted and simply returns no results.

parameters.name: pickupType
parameters.description:
**How the car should be handed over**, for a point or `locationId` search. Optional and
case-insensitive; `ALL`  -  every hand-over mode  -  is used when it is omitted.

- `ALL`  -  every car that serves the location, however it is handed over (default)
- `PICKUP_AT`  -  only cars handed over AT the location itself. At an airport this is the
  "meet me at the terminal" set
- `PICKUP_NEAR`  -  cars parked near the location, which the guest collects nearby

Which of the three a given place actually offers is published per location:
`/location-details` returns `availablePickupTypes` for each one (LAX publishes `PICKUP_AT`).

It applies to the point and `locationId` modes only. A bounding-box or country-wide search
ignores it  -  there is no single place to be picked up at.

Which of the three a given place actually offers is published per location:
`/location-details` returns `availablePickupTypes` for each one (LAX publishes `PICKUP_AT`).

It applies to the point and `locationId` modes only. A bounding-box or country-wide search
ignores it  -  there is no single place to be picked up at.

parameters.name: startDateTime
parameters.description:
**Trip start  -  when you want to pick the car up.** Format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm`, e.g.
`2026-09-10T10:00`. Optional, but see below.

**This is local time where the car is**  -  no time zone, no `Z`, no offset, no seconds.
"Pick up at 10:00" means 10:00 in the car's own city, which is what a rental means by it.
Adding a zone or an offset is rejected with a `400`.

**Searching without dates is allowed and returns a different kind of answer.** With no trip
window you get the catalogue: every car in the area with its typical daily price, but no
availability check and no trip-specific pricing (`availability` and `estimatedQuote` come
back empty). With a window you get what is actually bookable then, priced for those dates  - 
weekend and long-trip discounts included.

Send both `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` or neither; one on its own is a `400`.

For the exact, itemised price of one car over a window  -  daily rate, trip fee, taxes, young
driver fee  -  use `/trip-quote` once you have picked a car.

parameters.name: endDateTime
parameters.description:

`2026-09-14T10:00`. Optional; must be sent together with `startDateTime`.

Local time where the car is, exactly like `startDateTime`, and it must be after it.

reasonable default.

parameters.name: makes
parameters.description:
**Filter by manufacturer.** Optional; no make filter is applied when omitted.

Free text matched against Turo's own catalogue, and the catalogue is per-market  -  `/vehicle-makes`
returns the live list for a country (65 for `US`, 45 for `CA`), so read it there rather than
guessing a spelling. Values are the marque as Turo writes it: `Tesla`, `Ford`, `BMW`,
`Mercedes-Benz`, `Land Rover`, `AM General`.

Measured against the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline: `makes=Tesla` → 697.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

A make Turo does not know narrows the result set to nothing rather than erroring, so an empty
response with a non-zero `totalHits` elsewhere usually means a spelling that is not in
`/vehicle-makes`. Comma-separated.

parameters.name: features
parameters.description:
**Filter by the equipment a car has.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary of 21  -  anything else is rejected with a `400` naming the full set:

- Driving  -  `ALL_WHEEL_DRIVE`, `BLIND_SPOT_WARNING`, `BACKUP_CAMERA`, `KEYLESS_ENTRY`,
  `SNOW_TIRES`, `GPS`
- Phone & audio  -  `APPLE_CARPLAY`, `ANDROID_AUTO`, `BLUETOOTH`, `AUX_INPUT`, `USB_INPUT`,
  `USB_CHARGER`
- Comfort  -  `HEATED_SEATS`, `SUNROOF`, `CONVERTIBLE`, `ACCESSIBLE`
- Carrying things & people  -  `SKI_RACK`, `BIKE_RACK`, `CHILD_SEAT`, `PET_FRIENDLY`,
  `TOLL_PASS`

Measured: `features=ALL_WHEEL_DRIVE` → 2,339 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

`CONVERTIBLE` appears both here and in `types`  -  that is Turo's own doing, where a body style
and an amenity share a word. Either works.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

**Values inside this filter OR, which is worth stating twice here** because it reads like the
opposite: `features=SKI_RACK,BIKE_RACK` means "a ski rack OR a bike rack", not both. To
require two things at once, filter on one and check the other on the results  -  a car's full
equipment list is on `/vehicle-features`.

parameters.name: tmvTiers
parameters.description:
**Filter by Turo's own value tiering of a listing.** Optional; comma-separated.

A CLOSED vocabulary of three: `STANDARD`, `DELUXE`, `SUPER_DELUXE`. It is Turo's grading
of where a car sits in the market  -  roughly everyday, upmarket and luxury  -  and it is
the tiering the app's own price bands are built on.

All three are live. Measured against the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline: `STANDARD` → 7,151,
`DELUXE` → 1,018, `SUPER_DELUXE` → 251  -  so the three tiers partition the market almost
exactly, which makes this a good first cut when you want a whole market split into three
searches rather than a filter applied to one.

It is still a coarse instrument for shopping. For "nice cars" the `category` collections
(`SUPER_LUXE`, `RITZY_GERMAN`) are more precise, and for a hard budget the price band is more
precise still.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

parameters.name: category
parameters.description:
**Filter to one of Turo's curated collections.** Optional; one value only; case-insensitive.

These are the browse rows the Turo app itself shows  -  a hand-curated slice rather than a
mechanical filter.

**Use `/search-filters`'s `browseCollections` array to choose a value.** It contains the
collections that can be used by this parameter, together with their labels and artwork.

**There is no "all collections" value  -  omit the parameter instead.** `/search-filters`
lists `ALL` in its `categories` array, but that is the app's own "no collection" tab rather
than a filter value: sent as `category=ALL` the platform rejects the whole search with a
`400`. It is therefore not accepted here either, and leaving `category` off is what gives
you every car.

The live collections, with what each returned against the ~8,418-car baseline:

- Everyday  -  `BUDGET_FRIENDLY` (5,019), `COMPACT_CITY_CARS` (1,297), `FUEL_SIPPERS` (2,626)
- Space & practicality  -  `FAMILY_ROAD_TRIP` (4,121), `MOVING_DAY` (290),
  `CAR_CAMPING_ALL_START` (4,357), `RUGGED_4x4` (1,954)
- Upmarket  -  `RITZY_GERMAN` (1,499), `SUPER_LUXE` (302), `UK_FINEST` (183)
- Electric  -  `FASTEST_EV` (631), `ELECTRIC_ELITE` (145)
- Performance  -  `COMPACT_SPORTS` (408), `V8_ONLY` (477), `AMERICAN_SPORTS` (61),
  `MODERN_MUSCLE` (82), `MUSTANG_YEARS` (95), `SENSATIONAL_SUPERCARS` (35),
  `ITALIAN_STALLIONS` (15)
- Convertibles  -  `DROP_TOP` (487)
- Enthusiast & classic  -  `MANUALS_CLUB` (62), `CLASSIC_MUSCLE` (15), `VINTAGE_AMERICANA` (20),
  `NINETIES` (6)
- Gadgets  -  `ALL_GADGETS` (8,252), which is nearly the whole market

A collection is curated per market, so one that fills a row in Los Angeles can be thin or
empty in a smaller city  -  check `totalHits` rather than assuming a value is dead.

parameters.name: isAllStarHost
parameters.description:
**Only cars from All-Star Hosts.** Optional; no host-quality filter is applied when omitted.

All-Star Host is Turo's own recognition for hosts with consistently high ratings, fast
responses and few cancellations  -  the closest thing the platform has to a reliability
guarantee.

Measured: `isAllStarHost=true` → 3,586 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline, so it is a real
quality filter that still leaves a usable market rather than a decorative badge.

There is no way to ask for the inverse. Every result also carries its own `isAllStarHost`,
so the flag is checkable on the way out, and `/host-details` explains what a specific host
has earned.

parameters.name: minSeats
parameters.description:
**Minimum number of seats.** Optional; no seat floor is applied when omitted.

The car must seat at least this many people. Measured: `minSeats=7` → 1,382 of the 8,422 Los
Angeles baseline  -  the seven-seater market, which is what a family of six actually needs.

It is a floor, not an exact match: `minSeats=5` includes 7- and 8-seaters. Typical values are
`2` (sports cars and up), `4`, `5`, `7`, `8`.

Pair it with `types=MINIVAN,LARGE_SUV,PASSENGER_VAN` when you want space AND the right body
style  -  the seat count alone will also hand you a pickup truck with a rear bench.

parameters.name: age
parameters.description:
**The driver's age.** Optional; no age filter is applied when omitted.

Turo hosts set their own minimum renter age, and the platform prices young drivers
differently, so sending the real age of whoever will drive filters out the cars they are not
allowed to book  -  and prices the rest for them.

The thresholds that matter in the United States are 18, 21 and 25; a 21-year-old sees a
noticeably smaller market and higher prices than a 30-year-old in the same city.

Omit it and you get the unfiltered market, which is the right choice when you are surveying
inventory rather than booking a specific trip. `/vehicle-details` returns the exact
`minimumAgeInYearsToRent` for any single car.

not the registration date.

parameters.name: maxYear
parameters.description:
**Newest model year to include.** Optional; no upper year bound when omitted.

Send it with `minYear` to get a band, or alone for "this year or older". Measured with
`minYear=1990`: `maxYear=2000` → 8 cars.

Must be greater than or equal to `minYear`. Equal bounds select one model year; an
inverted band returns a `400` naming both values.

parameters.name: minPrice
parameters.description:
**Lowest price to include**, in the market's own currency. Optional.

**Read `priceType` before using this**  -  it decides whether the band is a DAILY rate or a
WHOLE-TRIP total, and the default is daily.

Verified end to end: `minPrice=50&maxPrice=100` on the default `DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`
returned cars from `50.42` to `99.02` a day  -  the band is applied to the daily rate, exactly
as documented. A `150` - `300` daily band narrowed the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline to 409.

Either bound works alone: `minPrice=100` with no `maxPrice` means "100 and up".

**Send a trip window with a price band.** With `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` the band is
applied exactly  -  verified twice: a `50` - `100` band returned `50.42` - `99.02` a day in Los
Angeles and `50.45` - `100.24` in London. Without dates there is no trip for the platform to
price, and the band becomes approximate: the same `50` - `100` band with no window returned
cars from `37.50` to `181.65`, with 24 of the 200 rows outside the band. It still narrows the
market usefully  -  it just is not a guarantee.

**Price bands are also the best way around the 200-car response cap.** Split the range into
disjoint slices (`0` - `50`, `50` - `100`, `100` - `200`, …) and search each: the slices do not
overlap, so the results add up to a full walk of the market that no paging parameter can
give you.

**The band is always in the currency of the market you are searching**  -  `USD`, `CAD`, `GBP`,
`AUD`, `EUR`  -  and every result carries its own `avgDailyPrice.currency`. Verified: a
`50` - `100` band on `country=GB` filters against pounds, returning cars at `50.45` - `100.24`
GBP. There is no currency parameter and no conversion.

parameters.name: priceType
parameters.description:
**What `minPrice` and `maxPrice` mean.** Optional; case-insensitive; defaults to
`DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`.

- `DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`  -  the band is a **daily rate** (default). Verified: `50` - `100`
  returned cars priced `50.42` - `99.02` per day
- `TOTAL`  -  the band is the **whole-trip total** for the window in `startDateTime` /
  `endDateTime`, which is the number a guest actually pays. Only meaningful with dates: with
  no trip window there is no total to compare against
- `MONTHLY`  -  the band is a monthly figure for longer rentals. Send the real trip dates so
  the results are priced for the stay you are comparing

Ignored unless at least one of `minPrice` / `maxPrice` is sent.

**The two are not interchangeable.** A four-day trip under a `100` daily cap can total 400
plus fees, so a customer shopping to a trip budget wants `TOTAL`, and a customer comparing
cars wants the daily rate. For the exact itemisation of one car  -  daily rate, trip fee,
taxes, young-driver fee  -  call `/trip-quote`.

parameters.name: unlimitedMileageOnly
parameters.description:
**Only cars with unlimited miles included.** Optional; no mileage filter when omitted.

Most Turo listings include a daily mileage allowance and charge per mile beyond it. Set this
to `true` to keep only the listings with no cap at all  -  the ones to book for a road trip,
where an overage charge is the difference between a good price and a bad one.

Measured: `unlimitedMileageOnly=true` → 470 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline. It is a harsh
filter, and that is the real shape of the market rather than an artefact.

**There is deliberately no "maximum mileage" or "at least N miles" parameter.** Turo does
not expose a limited-mileage threshold because its behavior is not established. Each result
carries its own mileage allowance, so an "at least
200 miles a day" rule can be applied to the rows on the way out.

parameters.name: minFuelEconomy
parameters.description:
**Minimum fuel economy**, in miles per gallon. Optional; no economy floor when omitted.

A floor. Measured: `minFuelEconomy=35` → 1,151 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

`/search-filters` publishes the tiers the Turo app itself offers for the market you are
searching (`fuelEfficiencyProperties.options`, e.g. "25+ MPG  -  Good"), which are a good guide
to values that split the market usefully.

 **An economy bound of ANY value drops every listing that carries no economy figure, and
that is most of the electric market.** Measured: the 8,410-car Los Angeles baseline falls to
**7,013** under `minFuelEconomy=0`, so a floor of zero  -  which reads like "no filter at all"  - 
already removes 1,397 cars. Cross-checked against the engine filter: `engines=ELECTRIC` alone
is 992 cars, but `minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is **1**. A couple of hundred petrol
listings have no figure either (`engines=GAS` 6,185 → 5,976 with a zero floor). So an economy
bound is a petrol/diesel/hybrid question  -  use `engines=ELECTRIC` for the electric market
instead, and never send a `0` bound as a no-op.

Pair it with `maxFuelEconomy` for a band. A single car's city, highway and combined figures,
and its battery range, are on `/vehicle-features`.

parameters.name: maxFuelEconomy
parameters.description:
**Maximum fuel economy**, in miles per gallon. Optional; no economy ceiling when omitted.

A ceiling  -  the mirror of `minFuelEconomy`. Measured against the 8,410-car Los Angeles
baseline: `maxFuelEconomy=24` → **2,208**, `maxFuelEconomy=15` → **79**, and
`maxFuelEconomy=200` (the ceiling this parameter accepts) → **7,013**, which is every listing
that carries an economy figure at all  -  the same count a `minFuelEconomy=0` floor returns.
`maxFuelEconomy=0` → **0**.

Either bound works alone, and they combine into a band: `minFuelEconomy=16&maxFuelEconomy=24`
→ **2,111**, against **4,604** for `minFuelEconomy=25` on its own. The bands are disjoint, so
the bound genuinely partitions the market rather than overlapping slices of it.

**Two things it is actually for.** First, finding the thirsty end of the market  -  the V8s and
the big trucks, which no other filter isolates. Second, **walking past the 200-car response
cap**: split the economy range into disjoint bands (`0` - `15`, `16` - `24`, `25` - `200`) and
search each, exactly the way `minPrice`/`maxPrice` bands are used for the same purpose. The
bands do not overlap, so the results add up rather than repeating.

 **Same caveat as `minFuelEconomy`: any economy bound drops every listing with no economy
figure**, which is nearly the whole electric market  -  `engines=ELECTRIC` is 992 cars, but
`minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is 1. Read that parameter's note before banding.

parameters.name: sortType
parameters.description:
**Result ordering.** Optional and case-insensitive; Turo's own relevance ranking is used when
omitted.

- `RELEVANCE`  -  Turo's blended ranking of price, rating, distance and popularity. This is
  what the app shows
- `PRICE`  -  by price. **The single most useful ordering on this API**, because a response is
  capped at 200 cars: `sortDirection=ASC` gives you the cheapest 200 of the match set and
  `DESC` the most expensive 200 of the same set. Verified in Los Angeles: `ASC` returned
  `18.02` - `33.05` a day, `DESC` returned `208.65` - `2956.50`
- `DISTANCE`  -  nearest first, measured from the point you searched. Only meaningful for a
  point or `locationId` search; every result carries its own `location.distance`
- `SCORE`  -  Turo's quality score, highest first
- `RANDOMIZED`  -  deliberately shuffled. Useful for sampling a market, useless for anything
  you intend to repeat

Anything else is rejected with a `400`. `/search-filters` publishes the orderings the app
offers for a market, with their labels.

**Sorting never returns more cars  -  it returns different ones.** The cap is 200 either way;
the ordering decides which 200 of the `totalHits` matches you see.

**Repeatability, measured.** Two identical `RELEVANCE` searches returned the same 200 cars in
the same order, so the default view is stable enough to diff between runs. `PRICE` returns the
same 200 cars but re-orders cars that share a price between calls  -  the membership is stable,
the order within a tie is not, so compare sets rather than positions.

parameters.name: sortDirection
parameters.description:
**Which way to sort.** Optional; `ASC` (ascending) or `DESC` (descending); case-insensitive.

Only meaningful alongside `sortType`. With `sortType=PRICE`: `ASC` is cheapest-first and
`DESC` is most-expensive-first  -  verified as `18.02` - `33.05` and `208.65` - `2956.50` a day on
the same Los Angeles search.

**Run both directions to read both ends of a market in two calls.** Because each response is
capped at 200 cars, one `PRICE ASC` call plus one `PRICE DESC` call gives you the budget end
and the luxury end of the same match set, with `totalHits` telling you how big the middle
you did not see is.

parameters.name: flexibleType
parameters.description:
**How strictly to apply your dates.** Optional; case-insensitive; only meaningful with
`startDateTime` and `endDateTime`.

- `FLEXIBLE_DEFAULT`  -  Turo may include cars that are close to, rather than exactly, your
  window. Useful when you are shopping for a price rather than committed to two dates
- `NOT_FLEXIBLE`  -  only cars available for exactly the window you asked for. This is the one
  to send when the response is going in front of someone about to book

With no dates at all there is nothing to be flexible about and the parameter has no effect.

**Measured caveat, stated rather than implied.** The platform genuinely parses this field  - 
an unrecognised value is rejected by its own validator  -  but on a dated Los Angeles search
both values returned the identical 8,418 matches. Treat it as a hint the platform is free to
ignore in a dense market, not as a hard availability filter: for a definitive yes/no on one
car and one window, call `/vehicle-availability`.

latitude.description:
**Latitude of the point to search around** (decimal degrees, WGS84).

Must be sent together with `longitude`. Examples: `34.0522` (Los Angeles), `40.7128` (New
York), `51.5074` (London, with `country=GB`), `43.6532` (Toronto, with `country=CA`).

Turo picks the radius itself from the density of cars around the point and echoes it back as
`searchLocation.appliedRadius`  -  about 34 miles around downtown Los Angeles. There is no
radius parameter to override it; use the bounding box when you need to control the area.

Range `-90` to `90`.

**Pick exactly ONE of the four ways to say where.** Mixing two returns a `400` naming the
conflict rather than quietly picking one for you:

- **A point**  -  `latitude` + `longitude`. Searches outward from a coordinate; each result carries
  its own `location.distance` back from that point, and the response echoes the radius Turo chose
  (`searchLocation.appliedRadius`, ~34 miles for a Los Angeles city centre point)
- **A bounding box**  -  `bottomLeftLatitude` + `bottomLeftLongitude` + `topRightLatitude` +
  `topRightLongitude`. Searches a rectangle, which is the right shape for a map viewport and the
  only way to tile a big market into pieces that each fit inside the 200-car response
- **A Turo pick-up location**  -  `locationId`, the numeric id of an airport or point of interest
  (`7894482` is LAX). Get one from `/location-details`, and use `pickupType` with it to say
  whether you want cars handed over AT that location or merely near it
- **A whole market**  -  `country` on its own, nothing else. Useful for "how much inventory is
  there in this country" (`totalHits`) rather than for browsing

`country` is required in all four modes  -  it selects the market, its currency and its catalogue.
Send half a pair (a `latitude` with no `longitude`, or three of the four box corners) and you get
a `400` naming the missing half rather than a silently different search.

longitude.description:

moves the search to another continent and returns an empty result set rather than an error.
Examples: `-118.2437` (Los Angeles), `-74.0060` (New York), `-0.1278` (London), `-79.3832`
(Toronto).

Range `-180` to `180`.

bottomLeftLatitude.description:
**South edge of the search rectangle** (decimal degrees). Part of the bounding-box mode.

All four corners  -  `bottomLeftLatitude`, `bottomLeftLongitude`, `topRightLatitude`,
`topRightLongitude`  -  must be sent together; three of the four is a `400`.

A worked box around Los Angeles: `bottomLeftLatitude=33.90`, `bottomLeftLongitude=-118.45`,
`topRightLatitude=34.20`, `topRightLongitude=-118.10`.

returns at most 200 cars, the way to enumerate a city is to cut it into tiles and search each

still above 200. The tiles do not overlap, so the results add up cleanly.

  there in this country" (`totalHits`) rather than for browsing

`country` is required in all four modes  -  it selects the market, its currency and its catalogue.
Send half a pair (a `latitude` with no `longitude`, or three of the four box corners) and you get

bottomLeftLongitude.description:

locationId.description:
**Numeric id of a Turo pick-up location**  -  an airport or a point of interest Turo hands
cars over at. This is the airport-rental mode.

Example: `7894482` is Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Ids come from
`/location-details`, which turns a place suggestion from `/location-autocomplete` into a
Turo location record carrying `locationId`, its coordinates and its
`availablePickupTypes`.

**Why use it instead of the airport's coordinates:** a `locationId` search is the airport
inventory as Turo itself defines it  -  the cars whose hosts have agreed to meet guests at that
terminal  -  rather than "every car within a radius of the runway". Pair it with `pickupType`
to choose between the two.

If you only have a place name, `/search-by-place` does the lookup and the search in one call.

**Pick exactly ONE of the four ways to say where.** Mixing two returns a `400` naming the
conflict rather than quietly picking one for you:

- **A point**  -  `latitude` + `longitude`. Searches outward from a coordinate; each result carries
  its own `location.distance` back from that point, and the response echoes the radius Turo chose
  (`searchLocation.appliedRadius`, ~34 miles for a Los Angeles city centre point)

  `topRightLongitude`. Searches a rectangle, which is the right shape for a map viewport and the

- **A Turo pick-up location**  -  `locationId`, the numeric id of an airport or point of interest
  (`7894482` is LAX). Get one from `/location-details`, and use `pickupType` with it to say
  whether you want cars handed over AT that location or merely near it
- **A whole market**  -  `country` on its own, nothing else. Useful for "how much inventory is
  there in this country" (`totalHits`) rather than for browsing

`country` is required in all four modes  -  it selects the market, its currency and its catalogue.
Send half a pair (a `latitude` with no `longitude`, or three of the four box corners) and you get
a `400` naming the missing half rather than a silently different search.

country.description:
**Market  -  a 2-letter ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 country code.** Case-insensitive.

Five markets carry inventory: `US`, `CA`, `GB`, `AU`, `FR`. Prices come back in that market's
currency (`USD`, `CAD`, `GBP`, `AUD`, `EUR`) and the make/model catalogue differs per market  - 
`/vehicle-makes` returns 65 makes for `US` and 45 for `CA`.

Any other valid code is accepted and simply returns no results.

pickupType.description:
**How the car should be handed over**, for a point or `locationId` search. Optional and
case-insensitive; `ALL`  -  every hand-over mode  -  is used when it is omitted.

- `ALL`  -  every car that serves the location, however it is handed over (default)
- `PICKUP_AT`  -  only cars handed over AT the location itself. At an airport this is the
  "meet me at the terminal" set
- `PICKUP_NEAR`  -  cars parked near the location, which the guest collects nearby

Which of the three a given place actually offers is published per location:
`/location-details` returns `availablePickupTypes` for each one (LAX publishes `PICKUP_AT`).

It applies to the point and `locationId` modes only. A bounding-box or country-wide search
ignores it  -  there is no single place to be picked up at.

startDateTime.description:
**Trip start  -  when you want to pick the car up.** Format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm`, e.g.
`2026-09-10T10:00`. Optional, but see below.

**This is local time where the car is**  -  no time zone, no `Z`, no offset, no seconds.
"Pick up at 10:00" means 10:00 in the car's own city, which is what a rental means by it.
Adding a zone or an offset is rejected with a `400`.

**Searching without dates is allowed and returns a different kind of answer.** With no trip
window you get the catalogue: every car in the area with its typical daily price, but no
availability check and no trip-specific pricing (`availability` and `estimatedQuote` come
back empty). With a window you get what is actually bookable then, priced for those dates  - 
weekend and long-trip discounts included.

Send both `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` or neither; one on its own is a `400`.

For the exact, itemised price of one car over a window  -  daily rate, trip fee, taxes, young
driver fee  -  use `/trip-quote` once you have picked a car.

endDateTime.description:
**Trip end  -  when you want to return the car.** Format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm`, e.g.
`2026-09-14T10:00`. Optional; must be sent together with `startDateTime`.

Local time where the car is, exactly like `startDateTime`, and it must be after it.

**Trip length changes the price, not just the total.** Turo hosts publish weekly and monthly
discounts, so the average daily rate on a 7-day window is routinely lower than on a 2-day
one for the same car. If you are comparing markets or tracking prices over time, hold the
trip length constant  -  the four-day window used for every measured figure in these docs is a
reasonable default.

makes.description:
**Filter by manufacturer.** Optional; no make filter is applied when omitted.

Free text matched against Turo's own catalogue, and the catalogue is per-market  -  `/vehicle-makes`
returns the live list for a country (65 for `US`, 45 for `CA`), so read it there rather than
guessing a spelling. Values are the marque as Turo writes it: `Tesla`, `Ford`, `BMW`,
`Mercedes-Benz`, `Land Rover`, `AM General`.

Measured against the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline: `makes=Tesla` → 697.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

A make Turo does not know narrows the result set to nothing rather than erroring, so an empty
response with a non-zero `totalHits` elsewhere usually means a spelling that is not in
`/vehicle-makes`. Comma-separated.

models.description:
**Filter by model.** Optional; no model filter is applied when omitted.

**Send it together with `makes`.** Model names are only unique inside a marque, and `/vehicle-models`
takes a `make` for that reason: `/vehicle-models?make=Tesla&country=US` returns `Model 3`,
`Model S`, `Model X`, `Model Y`, `Cybertruck`. Read the list there rather than guessing
punctuation and spacing.

Measured: `makes=Tesla` alone → 697 of the 8,422 baseline; adding `models=Model 3` → 292.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292. Comma-separated.

types.description:
**Filter by body style.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary  -  anything else is rejected with a `400` naming the accepted values:

- Cars  -  `CAR`, `SEDAN`, `COUPE`, `HATCHBACK_WAGON`, `CONVERTIBLE`
- SUVs  -  `SUV`, `COMPACT_SUV`, `MIDSIZE_SUV`, `LARGE_SUV`
- Trucks & vans  -  `TRUCK`, `BOX_TRUCK`, `VAN`, `CARGO_VAN`, `PASSENGER_VAN`, `MINIVAN`,
  `CARGO_MINIVAN`, `PASSENGER_MINIVAN`

Measured: `types=TRUCK` → 241 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

`/search-filters` publishes the same vocabulary grouped the way the Turo app groups it, with
the human label for each value.

engines.description:
**Filter by what the car burns.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary of four. Measured against the
8,418-car Los Angeles baseline:

- `GAS`  -  6,192
- `HYBRID`  -  petrol-electric hybrids, 1,162
- `ELECTRIC`  -  battery electric, 992
- `DIESEL`  -  72
**For "anything but electric", send `engines=GAS,DIESEL,HYBRID`**  -  measured 7,426 of the
same baseline.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

For a specific car's battery range or its city/highway economy figures, `/vehicle-features`
returns them per listing.

features.description:
**Filter by the equipment a car has.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary of 21  -  anything else is rejected with a `400` naming the full set:

- Driving  -  `ALL_WHEEL_DRIVE`, `BLIND_SPOT_WARNING`, `BACKUP_CAMERA`, `KEYLESS_ENTRY`,
  `SNOW_TIRES`, `GPS`
- Phone & audio  -  `APPLE_CARPLAY`, `ANDROID_AUTO`, `BLUETOOTH`, `AUX_INPUT`, `USB_INPUT`,
  `USB_CHARGER`
- Comfort  -  `HEATED_SEATS`, `SUNROOF`, `CONVERTIBLE`, `ACCESSIBLE`
- Carrying things & people  -  `SKI_RACK`, `BIKE_RACK`, `CHILD_SEAT`, `PET_FRIENDLY`,
  `TOLL_PASS`

Measured: `features=ALL_WHEEL_DRIVE` → 2,339 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

`CONVERTIBLE` appears both here and in `types`  -  that is Turo's own doing, where a body style
and an amenity share a word. Either works.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

**Values inside this filter OR, which is worth stating twice here** because it reads like the
opposite: `features=SKI_RACK,BIKE_RACK` means "a ski rack OR a bike rack", not both. To
require two things at once, filter on one and check the other on the results  -  a car's full
equipment list is on `/vehicle-features`.

tmvTiers.description:
**Filter by Turo's own value tiering of a listing.** Optional; comma-separated.

A CLOSED vocabulary of three: `STANDARD`, `DELUXE`, `SUPER_DELUXE`. It is Turo's grading
of where a car sits in the market  -  roughly everyday, upmarket and luxury  -  and it is
the tiering the app's own price bands are built on.

All three are live. Measured against the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline: `STANDARD` → 7,151,
`DELUXE` → 1,018, `SUPER_DELUXE` → 251  -  so the three tiers partition the market almost
exactly, which makes this a good first cut when you want a whole market split into three
searches rather than a filter applied to one.

It is still a coarse instrument for shopping. For "nice cars" the `category` collections
(`SUPER_LUXE`, `RITZY_GERMAN`) are more precise, and for a hard budget the price band is more
precise still.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

category.description:
**Filter to one of Turo's curated collections.** Optional; one value only; case-insensitive.

These are the browse rows the Turo app itself shows  -  a hand-curated slice rather than a
mechanical filter.

**Use `/search-filters`'s `browseCollections` array to choose a value.** It contains the
collections that can be used by this parameter, together with their labels and artwork.

**There is no "all collections" value  -  omit the parameter instead.** `/search-filters`
lists `ALL` in its `categories` array, but that is the app's own "no collection" tab rather
than a filter value: sent as `category=ALL` the platform rejects the whole search with a
`400`. It is therefore not accepted here either, and leaving `category` off is what gives
you every car.

The live collections, with what each returned against the ~8,418-car baseline:

- Everyday  -  `BUDGET_FRIENDLY` (5,019), `COMPACT_CITY_CARS` (1,297), `FUEL_SIPPERS` (2,626)
- Space & practicality  -  `FAMILY_ROAD_TRIP` (4,121), `MOVING_DAY` (290),
  `CAR_CAMPING_ALL_START` (4,357), `RUGGED_4x4` (1,954)
- Upmarket  -  `RITZY_GERMAN` (1,499), `SUPER_LUXE` (302), `UK_FINEST` (183)
- Electric  -  `FASTEST_EV` (631), `ELECTRIC_ELITE` (145)
- Performance  -  `COMPACT_SPORTS` (408), `V8_ONLY` (477), `AMERICAN_SPORTS` (61),
  `MODERN_MUSCLE` (82), `MUSTANG_YEARS` (95), `SENSATIONAL_SUPERCARS` (35),
  `ITALIAN_STALLIONS` (15)
- Convertibles  -  `DROP_TOP` (487)
- Enthusiast & classic  -  `MANUALS_CLUB` (62), `CLASSIC_MUSCLE` (15), `VINTAGE_AMERICANA` (20),
  `NINETIES` (6)
- Gadgets  -  `ALL_GADGETS` (8,252), which is nearly the whole market

A collection is curated per market, so one that fills a row in Los Angeles can be thin or
empty in a smaller city  -  check `totalHits` rather than assuming a value is dead.

transmission.description:
**Filter by gearbox.** Optional; `AUTOMATIC` or `MANUAL`; case-insensitive.

Exactly two values are accepted  -  anything else is a `400`.

Measured: `transmission=MANUAL` → 63 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline. Manuals are genuinely
rare in North American markets, so an almost-empty result there is the real answer rather
than a broken filter; the same filter is far less brutal in `GB` and `FR`.

For enthusiast manuals specifically, `category=MANUALS_CLUB` is the curated row.

isAllStarHost.description:
**Only cars from All-Star Hosts.** Optional; no host-quality filter is applied when omitted.

All-Star Host is Turo's own recognition for hosts with consistently high ratings, fast
responses and few cancellations  -  the closest thing the platform has to a reliability
guarantee.

Measured: `isAllStarHost=true` → 3,586 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline, so it is a real
quality filter that still leaves a usable market rather than a decorative badge.

There is no way to ask for the inverse. Every result also carries its own `isAllStarHost`,
so the flag is checkable on the way out, and `/host-details` explains what a specific host
has earned.

minSeats.description:
**Minimum number of seats.** Optional; no seat floor is applied when omitted.

The car must seat at least this many people. Measured: `minSeats=7` → 1,382 of the 8,422 Los
Angeles baseline  -  the seven-seater market, which is what a family of six actually needs.

It is a floor, not an exact match: `minSeats=5` includes 7- and 8-seaters. Typical values are
`2` (sports cars and up), `4`, `5`, `7`, `8`.

Pair it with `types=MINIVAN,LARGE_SUV,PASSENGER_VAN` when you want space AND the right body
style  -  the seat count alone will also hand you a pickup truck with a rear bench.

age.description:
**The driver's age.** Optional; no age filter is applied when omitted.

Turo hosts set their own minimum renter age, and the platform prices young drivers
differently, so sending the real age of whoever will drive filters out the cars they are not
allowed to book  -  and prices the rest for them.

The thresholds that matter in the United States are 18, 21 and 25; a 21-year-old sees a
noticeably smaller market and higher prices than a 30-year-old in the same city.

Omit it and you get the unfiltered market, which is the right choice when you are surveying
inventory rather than booking a specific trip. `/vehicle-details` returns the exact
`minimumAgeInYearsToRent` for any single car.

minYear.description:
**Oldest model year to include.** Optional; no lower year bound when omitted.

Send it with `maxYear` to get a band. Measured: `minYear=1990&maxYear=2000` → 8 of the 8,422
Los Angeles baseline, which is the classic-car corner of the market.

Either bound works on its own: `minYear=2022` alone means "2022 or newer".

This is the model year Turo publishes for the listing (each result carries its own `year`),
not the registration date.

maxYear.description:
**Newest model year to include.** Optional; no upper year bound when omitted.

Send it with `minYear` to get a band, or alone for "this year or older". Measured with
`minYear=1990`: `maxYear=2000` → 8 cars.

Must be greater than or equal to `minYear`. Equal bounds select one model year; an
inverted band returns a `400` naming both values.

minPrice.description:
**Lowest price to include**, in the market's own currency. Optional.

**Read `priceType` before using this**  -  it decides whether the band is a DAILY rate or a
WHOLE-TRIP total, and the default is daily.

Verified end to end: `minPrice=50&maxPrice=100` on the default `DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`
returned cars from `50.42` to `99.02` a day  -  the band is applied to the daily rate, exactly
as documented. A `150` - `300` daily band narrowed the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline to 409.

Either bound works alone: `minPrice=100` with no `maxPrice` means "100 and up".

**Send a trip window with a price band.** With `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` the band is
applied exactly  -  verified twice: a `50` - `100` band returned `50.42` - `99.02` a day in Los
Angeles and `50.45` - `100.24` in London. Without dates there is no trip for the platform to
price, and the band becomes approximate: the same `50` - `100` band with no window returned
cars from `37.50` to `181.65`, with 24 of the 200 rows outside the band. It still narrows the
market usefully  -  it just is not a guarantee.

**Price bands are also the best way around the 200-car response cap.** Split the range into
disjoint slices (`0` - `50`, `50` - `100`, `100` - `200`, …) and search each: the slices do not
overlap, so the results add up to a full walk of the market that no paging parameter can
give you.

**The band is always in the currency of the market you are searching**  -  `USD`, `CAD`, `GBP`,
`AUD`, `EUR`  -  and every result carries its own `avgDailyPrice.currency`. Verified: a
`50` - `100` band on `country=GB` filters against pounds, returning cars at `50.45` - `100.24`
GBP. There is no currency parameter and no conversion.

maxPrice.description:
**Highest price to include**, in the market's own currency. Optional.

Interpreted by `priceType` the same way `minPrice` is  -  daily rate by default, whole-trip
total when you ask for it. Verified: `minPrice=50&maxPrice=100` returned daily rates from
`50.42` to `99.02`.

Either bound works alone: `maxPrice=75` with no `minPrice` means "75 and under".

**Send a trip window with a price band.** With `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` the band is
applied exactly  -  verified twice: a `50` - `100` band returned `50.42` - `99.02` a day in Los
Angeles and `50.45` - `100.24` in London. Without dates there is no trip for the platform to
price, and the band becomes approximate: the same `50` - `100` band with no window returned
cars from `37.50` to `181.65`, with 24 of the 200 rows outside the band. It still narrows the
market usefully  -  it just is not a guarantee.

**A budget is not the same question as a cheap search.** For "the cheapest cars here", sort
by price ascending instead  -  a `maxPrice` band plus a 200-car cap gives you 200 arbitrary
cars under the cap, while `sortType=PRICE&sortDirection=ASC` gives you the 200 cheapest in
order.

priceType.description:
**What `minPrice` and `maxPrice` mean.** Optional; case-insensitive; defaults to
`DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`.

- `DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`  -  the band is a **daily rate** (default). Verified: `50` - `100`
  returned cars priced `50.42` - `99.02` per day
- `TOTAL`  -  the band is the **whole-trip total** for the window in `startDateTime` /
  `endDateTime`, which is the number a guest actually pays. Only meaningful with dates: with
  no trip window there is no total to compare against
- `MONTHLY`  -  the band is a monthly figure for longer rentals. Send the real trip dates so
  the results are priced for the stay you are comparing

Ignored unless at least one of `minPrice` / `maxPrice` is sent.

**The two are not interchangeable.** A four-day trip under a `100` daily cap can total 400
plus fees, so a customer shopping to a trip budget wants `TOTAL`, and a customer comparing
cars wants the daily rate. For the exact itemisation of one car  -  daily rate, trip fee,
taxes, young-driver fee  -  call `/trip-quote`.

unlimitedMileageOnly.description:
**Only cars with unlimited miles included.** Optional; no mileage filter when omitted.

Most Turo listings include a daily mileage allowance and charge per mile beyond it. Set this
to `true` to keep only the listings with no cap at all  -  the ones to book for a road trip,
where an overage charge is the difference between a good price and a bad one.

Measured: `unlimitedMileageOnly=true` → 470 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline. It is a harsh
filter, and that is the real shape of the market rather than an artefact.

**There is deliberately no "maximum mileage" or "at least N miles" parameter.** Turo does
not expose a limited-mileage threshold because its behavior is not established. Each result
carries its own mileage allowance, so an "at least
200 miles a day" rule can be applied to the rows on the way out.

minFuelEconomy.description:
**Minimum fuel economy**, in miles per gallon. Optional; no economy floor when omitted.

A floor. Measured: `minFuelEconomy=35` → 1,151 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

`/search-filters` publishes the tiers the Turo app itself offers for the market you are
searching (`fuelEfficiencyProperties.options`, e.g. "25+ MPG  -  Good"), which are a good guide
to values that split the market usefully.

 **An economy bound of ANY value drops every listing that carries no economy figure, and
that is most of the electric market.** Measured: the 8,410-car Los Angeles baseline falls to
**7,013** under `minFuelEconomy=0`, so a floor of zero  -  which reads like "no filter at all"  - 
already removes 1,397 cars. Cross-checked against the engine filter: `engines=ELECTRIC` alone
is 992 cars, but `minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is **1**. A couple of hundred petrol
listings have no figure either (`engines=GAS` 6,185 → 5,976 with a zero floor). So an economy
bound is a petrol/diesel/hybrid question  -  use `engines=ELECTRIC` for the electric market
instead, and never send a `0` bound as a no-op.

Pair it with `maxFuelEconomy` for a band. A single car's city, highway and combined figures,
and its battery range, are on `/vehicle-features`.

maxFuelEconomy.description:
**Maximum fuel economy**, in miles per gallon. Optional; no economy ceiling when omitted.

A ceiling  -  the mirror of `minFuelEconomy`. Measured against the 8,410-car Los Angeles
baseline: `maxFuelEconomy=24` → **2,208**, `maxFuelEconomy=15` → **79**, and
`maxFuelEconomy=200` (the ceiling this parameter accepts) → **7,013**, which is every listing
that carries an economy figure at all  -  the same count a `minFuelEconomy=0` floor returns.
`maxFuelEconomy=0` → **0**.

Either bound works alone, and they combine into a band: `minFuelEconomy=16&maxFuelEconomy=24`
→ **2,111**, against **4,604** for `minFuelEconomy=25` on its own. The bands are disjoint, so
the bound genuinely partitions the market rather than overlapping slices of it.

**Two things it is actually for.** First, finding the thirsty end of the market  -  the V8s and
the big trucks, which no other filter isolates. Second, **walking past the 200-car response
cap**: split the economy range into disjoint bands (`0` - `15`, `16` - `24`, `25` - `200`) and
search each, exactly the way `minPrice`/`maxPrice` bands are used for the same purpose. The
bands do not overlap, so the results add up rather than repeating.

 **Same caveat as `minFuelEconomy`: any economy bound drops every listing with no economy
figure**, which is nearly the whole electric market  -  `engines=ELECTRIC` is 992 cars, but
`minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is 1. Read that parameter's note before banding.

sortType.description:
**Result ordering.** Optional and case-insensitive; Turo's own relevance ranking is used when
omitted.

- `RELEVANCE`  -  Turo's blended ranking of price, rating, distance and popularity. This is
  what the app shows
- `PRICE`  -  by price. **The single most useful ordering on this API**, because a response is
  capped at 200 cars: `sortDirection=ASC` gives you the cheapest 200 of the match set and
  `DESC` the most expensive 200 of the same set. Verified in Los Angeles: `ASC` returned
  `18.02` - `33.05` a day, `DESC` returned `208.65` - `2956.50`
- `DISTANCE`  -  nearest first, measured from the point you searched. Only meaningful for a
  point or `locationId` search; every result carries its own `location.distance`
- `SCORE`  -  Turo's quality score, highest first
- `RANDOMIZED`  -  deliberately shuffled. Useful for sampling a market, useless for anything
  you intend to repeat

Anything else is rejected with a `400`. `/search-filters` publishes the orderings the app
offers for a market, with their labels.

**Sorting never returns more cars  -  it returns different ones.** The cap is 200 either way;
the ordering decides which 200 of the `totalHits` matches you see.

**Repeatability, measured.** Two identical `RELEVANCE` searches returned the same 200 cars in
the same order, so the default view is stable enough to diff between runs. `PRICE` returns the
same 200 cars but re-orders cars that share a price between calls  -  the membership is stable,
the order within a tie is not, so compare sets rather than positions.

sortDirection.description:
**Which way to sort.** Optional; `ASC` (ascending) or `DESC` (descending); case-insensitive.

Only meaningful alongside `sortType`. With `sortType=PRICE`: `ASC` is cheapest-first and
`DESC` is most-expensive-first  -  verified as `18.02` - `33.05` and `208.65` - `2956.50` a day on
the same Los Angeles search.

**Run both directions to read both ends of a market in two calls.** Because each response is
capped at 200 cars, one `PRICE ASC` call plus one `PRICE DESC` call gives you the budget end
and the luxury end of the same match set, with `totalHits` telling you how big the middle
you did not see is.

flexibleType.description:
**How strictly to apply your dates.** Optional; case-insensitive; only meaningful with
`startDateTime` and `endDateTime`.

- `FLEXIBLE_DEFAULT`  -  Turo may include cars that are close to, rather than exactly, your
  window. Useful when you are shopping for a price rather than committed to two dates
- `NOT_FLEXIBLE`  -  only cars available for exactly the window you asked for. This is the one
  to send when the response is going in front of someone about to book

With no dates at all there is nothing to be flexible about and the parameter has no effect.

**Measured caveat, stated rather than implied.** The platform genuinely parses this field  - 
an unrecognised value is rejected by its own validator  -  but on a dated Los Angeles search
both values returned the identical 8,418 matches. Treat it as a hint the platform is free to
ignore in a dense market, not as a hard availability filter: for a definitive yes/no on one
car and one window, call `/vehicle-availability`.

description: Search cars by place name  -  "Los Angeles" or "LAX"  -  resolved and searched in one call.

parameters.name: place
parameters.description:
**Where to search, in plain words.** Required. A city, an airport code, a neighbourhood or an
address  -  whatever a person would type into a search box.

Examples that all resolve, measured: `Los Angeles`, `LAX`, `O'Hare`, `Miami Beach`,
`New York`, `London`, `Paris`, `Toronto`, `Sydney`, `Saint-Étienne`.

**Not every place name Turo suggests can be searched.** Turo autocompletes far more places than
it holds pick-up locations for, and a suggestion it cannot turn into a searchable location comes
back as a `404` saying so  -  measured, the New York boroughs are exactly this case: `Brooklyn`,
`Brooklyn, NY` and `Queens, NY` are all refused while `New York` a few miles away resolves
normally. Name the city rather than the district, or the airport, when that happens.

**Cities and airports resolve differently, and this endpoint hides the difference for you.** An
airport is a Turo pick-up location with its own id, so an airport name is searched as "cars
handed over at this airport". A city is a place on a map, so a city name is searched as a point
with the radius Turo picks for it. Doing that by hand takes two or three calls
(`/location-autocomplete`, then `/location-details`, then `/search`); here it is one.

The best match is used, and **the market is taken from the place itself** unless you override it
with `country`: `London` is searched in `GB`, `Paris` in `FR`, `Toronto` in `CA` and `Sydney` in
`AU` with no `country` at all, and the market that answered is reported back on
`resolvedLocation.country`. Send `country` to disambiguate a name that exists in several markets
 -  `Birmingham`, `Cambridge`, `Perth`, `Melbourne`  -  or when the first match is not the one you
meant; an explicit market always wins.

**A name nothing matches returns a `404` saying so**, rather than an empty car list that reads
like "no cars here". If you need to see the candidates and choose yourself, call
`/location-autocomplete` and pass the winner's coordinates or `locationId` to `/search`.

parameters.name: country
parameters.description:
**Market  -  a 2-letter ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 country code.** Optional here, and case-insensitive.

Five markets carry inventory: `US`, `CA`, `GB`, `AU`, `FR`. Prices come back in that market's
currency and the make/model catalogue differs per market.

Leave it off and the market is taken from what you supplied  -  the place you named, or the
link you pasted. Send it to override that, or to disambiguate a place name that exists in
more than one country (`Birmingham`, `Cambridge`, `Perth`).

parameters.name: pickupType
parameters.description:
**How the car should be handed over**, for a point or `locationId` search. Optional and
case-insensitive; `ALL`  -  every hand-over mode  -  is used when it is omitted.

- `ALL`  -  every car that serves the location, however it is handed over (default)
- `PICKUP_AT`  -  only cars handed over AT the location itself. At an airport this is the
  "meet me at the terminal" set
- `PICKUP_NEAR`  -  cars parked near the location, which the guest collects nearby

Which of the three a given place actually offers is published per location:
`/location-details` returns `availablePickupTypes` for each one (LAX publishes `PICKUP_AT`).

It applies to the point and `locationId` modes only. A bounding-box or country-wide search
ignores it  -  there is no single place to be picked up at.

parameters.name: startDateTime
parameters.description:
**Trip start  -  when you want to pick the car up.** Format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm`, e.g.
`2026-09-10T10:00`. Optional, but see below.

**This is local time where the car is**  -  no time zone, no `Z`, no offset, no seconds.
"Pick up at 10:00" means 10:00 in the car's own city, which is what a rental means by it.
Adding a zone or an offset is rejected with a `400`.

**Searching without dates is allowed and returns a different kind of answer.** With no trip
window you get the catalogue: every car in the area with its typical daily price, but no
availability check and no trip-specific pricing (`availability` and `estimatedQuote` come
back empty). With a window you get what is actually bookable then, priced for those dates  - 
weekend and long-trip discounts included.

Send both `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` or neither; one on its own is a `400`.

For the exact, itemised price of one car over a window  -  daily rate, trip fee, taxes, young
driver fee  -  use `/trip-quote` once you have picked a car.

parameters.name: endDateTime
parameters.description:
**Trip end  -  when you want to return the car.** Format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm`, e.g.
`2026-09-14T10:00`. Optional; must be sent together with `startDateTime`.

Local time where the car is, exactly like `startDateTime`, and it must be after it.

**Trip length changes the price, not just the total.** Turo hosts publish weekly and monthly
discounts, so the average daily rate on a 7-day window is routinely lower than on a 2-day
one for the same car. If you are comparing markets or tracking prices over time, hold the
trip length constant  -  the four-day window used for every measured figure in these docs is a
reasonable default.

parameters.name: makes
parameters.description:
**Filter by manufacturer.** Optional; no make filter is applied when omitted.

Free text matched against Turo's own catalogue, and the catalogue is per-market  -  `/vehicle-makes`
returns the live list for a country (65 for `US`, 45 for `CA`), so read it there rather than
guessing a spelling. Values are the marque as Turo writes it: `Tesla`, `Ford`, `BMW`,
`Mercedes-Benz`, `Land Rover`, `AM General`.

Measured against the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline: `makes=Tesla` → 697.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

A make Turo does not know narrows the result set to nothing rather than erroring, so an empty
response with a non-zero `totalHits` elsewhere usually means a spelling that is not in
`/vehicle-makes`. Comma-separated.

punctuation and spacing.

Measured: `makes=Tesla` alone → 697 of the 8,422 baseline; adding `models=Model 3` → 292.

parameters.name: types
parameters.description:
**Filter by body style.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary  -  anything else is rejected with a `400` naming the accepted values:

- Cars  -  `CAR`, `SEDAN`, `COUPE`, `HATCHBACK_WAGON`, `CONVERTIBLE`
- SUVs  -  `SUV`, `COMPACT_SUV`, `MIDSIZE_SUV`, `LARGE_SUV`
- Trucks & vans  -  `TRUCK`, `BOX_TRUCK`, `VAN`, `CARGO_VAN`, `PASSENGER_VAN`, `MINIVAN`,
  `CARGO_MINIVAN`, `PASSENGER_MINIVAN`

Measured: `types=TRUCK` → 241 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

`/search-filters` publishes the same vocabulary grouped the way the Turo app groups it, with
the human label for each value.

parameters.name: engines
parameters.description:
**Filter by what the car burns.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary of four. Measured against the
8,418-car Los Angeles baseline:

- `GAS`  -  6,192

- `DIESEL`  -  72

returns them per listing.

parameters.name: features
parameters.description:
**Filter by the equipment a car has.** Optional; comma-separated; case-insensitive.

A CLOSED vocabulary of 21  -  anything else is rejected with a `400` naming the full set:

- Driving  -  `ALL_WHEEL_DRIVE`, `BLIND_SPOT_WARNING`, `BACKUP_CAMERA`, `KEYLESS_ENTRY`,
  `SNOW_TIRES`, `GPS`
- Phone & audio  -  `APPLE_CARPLAY`, `ANDROID_AUTO`, `BLUETOOTH`, `AUX_INPUT`, `USB_INPUT`,
  `USB_CHARGER`
- Comfort  -  `HEATED_SEATS`, `SUNROOF`, `CONVERTIBLE`, `ACCESSIBLE`
- Carrying things & people  -  `SKI_RACK`, `BIKE_RACK`, `CHILD_SEAT`, `PET_FRIENDLY`,
  `TOLL_PASS`

Measured: `features=ALL_WHEEL_DRIVE` → 2,339 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

`CONVERTIBLE` appears both here and in `types`  -  that is Turo's own doing, where a body style
and an amenity share a word. Either works.

equipment list is on `/vehicle-features`.

parameters.name: tmvTiers
parameters.description:
**Filter by Turo's own value tiering of a listing.** Optional; comma-separated.

A CLOSED vocabulary of three: `STANDARD`, `DELUXE`, `SUPER_DELUXE`. It is Turo's grading
of where a car sits in the market  -  roughly everyday, upmarket and luxury  -  and it is
the tiering the app's own price bands are built on.

All three are live. Measured against the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline: `STANDARD` → 7,151,
`DELUXE` → 1,018, `SUPER_DELUXE` → 251  -  so the three tiers partition the market almost
exactly, which makes this a good first cut when you want a whole market split into three
searches rather than a filter applied to one.

It is still a coarse instrument for shopping. For "nice cars" the `category` collections
(`SUPER_LUXE`, `RITZY_GERMAN`) are more precise, and for a hard budget the price band is more
precise still.

**How values combine:** values inside ONE filter are combined with **OR**; different filters are
combined with **AND**. So adding values to this filter WIDENS the result set, and adding another
filter NARROWS it. Measured: `makes=Tesla` returned 697 of the 8,422 baseline, and adding
`models=Model 3` to it narrowed that to 292.

parameters.name: category
parameters.description:
**Filter to one of Turo's curated collections.** Optional; one value only; case-insensitive.

These are the browse rows the Turo app itself shows  -  a hand-curated slice rather than a
mechanical filter.

**Use `/search-filters`'s `browseCollections` array to choose a value.** It contains the
collections that can be used by this parameter, together with their labels and artwork.

**There is no "all collections" value  -  omit the parameter instead.** `/search-filters`
lists `ALL` in its `categories` array, but that is the app's own "no collection" tab rather
than a filter value: sent as `category=ALL` the platform rejects the whole search with a
`400`. It is therefore not accepted here either, and leaving `category` off is what gives
you every car.

The live collections, with what each returned against the ~8,418-car baseline:

- Everyday  -  `BUDGET_FRIENDLY` (5,019), `COMPACT_CITY_CARS` (1,297), `FUEL_SIPPERS` (2,626)
- Space & practicality  -  `FAMILY_ROAD_TRIP` (4,121), `MOVING_DAY` (290),
  `CAR_CAMPING_ALL_START` (4,357), `RUGGED_4x4` (1,954)
- Upmarket  -  `RITZY_GERMAN` (1,499), `SUPER_LUXE` (302), `UK_FINEST` (183)
- Electric  -  `FASTEST_EV` (631), `ELECTRIC_ELITE` (145)
- Performance  -  `COMPACT_SPORTS` (408), `V8_ONLY` (477), `AMERICAN_SPORTS` (61),
  `MODERN_MUSCLE` (82), `MUSTANG_YEARS` (95), `SENSATIONAL_SUPERCARS` (35),
  `ITALIAN_STALLIONS` (15)
- Convertibles  -  `DROP_TOP` (487)
- Enthusiast & classic  -  `MANUALS_CLUB` (62), `CLASSIC_MUSCLE` (15), `VINTAGE_AMERICANA` (20),
  `NINETIES` (6)
- Gadgets  -  `ALL_GADGETS` (8,252), which is nearly the whole market

A collection is curated per market, so one that fills a row in Los Angeles can be thin or
empty in a smaller city  -  check `totalHits` rather than assuming a value is dead.

parameters.name: transmission
parameters.description:
**Filter by gearbox.** Optional; `AUTOMATIC` or `MANUAL`; case-insensitive.

Exactly two values are accepted  -  anything else is a `400`.

parameters.name: isAllStarHost
parameters.description:
**Only cars from All-Star Hosts.** Optional; no host-quality filter is applied when omitted.

All-Star Host is Turo's own recognition for hosts with consistently high ratings, fast
responses and few cancellations  -  the closest thing the platform has to a reliability
guarantee.

Measured: `isAllStarHost=true` → 3,586 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline, so it is a real
quality filter that still leaves a usable market rather than a decorative badge.

There is no way to ask for the inverse. Every result also carries its own `isAllStarHost`,
so the flag is checkable on the way out, and `/host-details` explains what a specific host
has earned.

parameters.name: minSeats
parameters.description:
**Minimum number of seats.** Optional; no seat floor is applied when omitted.

The car must seat at least this many people. Measured: `minSeats=7` → 1,382 of the 8,422 Los
Angeles baseline  -  the seven-seater market, which is what a family of six actually needs.

It is a floor, not an exact match: `minSeats=5` includes 7- and 8-seaters. Typical values are
`2` (sports cars and up), `4`, `5`, `7`, `8`.

Pair it with `types=MINIVAN,LARGE_SUV,PASSENGER_VAN` when you want space AND the right body
style  -  the seat count alone will also hand you a pickup truck with a rear bench.

parameters.name: age
parameters.description:
**The driver's age.** Optional; no age filter is applied when omitted.

Turo hosts set their own minimum renter age, and the platform prices young drivers
differently, so sending the real age of whoever will drive filters out the cars they are not
allowed to book  -  and prices the rest for them.

The thresholds that matter in the United States are 18, 21 and 25; a 21-year-old sees a
noticeably smaller market and higher prices than a 30-year-old in the same city.

Omit it and you get the unfiltered market, which is the right choice when you are surveying
inventory rather than booking a specific trip. `/vehicle-details` returns the exact
`minimumAgeInYearsToRent` for any single car.

**Oldest model year to include.** Optional; no lower year bound when omitted.

Send it with `maxYear` to get a band. Measured: `minYear=1990&maxYear=2000` → 8 of the 8,422
Los Angeles baseline, which is the classic-car corner of the market.

Either bound works on its own: `minYear=2022` alone means "2022 or newer".

This is the model year Turo publishes for the listing (each result carries its own `year`),
not the registration date.

Send it with `minYear` to get a band, or alone for "this year or older". Measured with

parameters.name: minPrice
parameters.description:
**Lowest price to include**, in the market's own currency. Optional.

**Read `priceType` before using this**  -  it decides whether the band is a DAILY rate or a
WHOLE-TRIP total, and the default is daily.

Verified end to end: `minPrice=50&maxPrice=100` on the default `DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`
returned cars from `50.42` to `99.02` a day  -  the band is applied to the daily rate, exactly
as documented. A `150` - `300` daily band narrowed the 8,422-car Los Angeles baseline to 409.

Either bound works alone: `minPrice=100` with no `maxPrice` means "100 and up".

**Send a trip window with a price band.** With `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` the band is
applied exactly  -  verified twice: a `50` - `100` band returned `50.42` - `99.02` a day in Los
Angeles and `50.45` - `100.24` in London. Without dates there is no trip for the platform to
price, and the band becomes approximate: the same `50` - `100` band with no window returned
cars from `37.50` to `181.65`, with 24 of the 200 rows outside the band. It still narrows the
market usefully  -  it just is not a guarantee.

**Price bands are also the best way around the 200-car response cap.** Split the range into
disjoint slices (`0` - `50`, `50` - `100`, `100` - `200`, …) and search each: the slices do not
overlap, so the results add up to a full walk of the market that no paging parameter can
give you.

**The band is always in the currency of the market you are searching**  -  `USD`, `CAD`, `GBP`,
`AUD`, `EUR`  -  and every result carries its own `avgDailyPrice.currency`. Verified: a
`50` - `100` band on `country=GB` filters against pounds, returning cars at `50.45` - `100.24`
GBP. There is no currency parameter and no conversion.

parameters.description:

Interpreted by `priceType` the same way `minPrice` is  -  daily rate by default, whole-trip
total when you ask for it. Verified: `minPrice=50&maxPrice=100` returned daily rates from

**Send a trip window with a price band.** With `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` the band is

by price ascending instead  -  a `maxPrice` band plus a 200-car cap gives you 200 arbitrary
cars under the cap, while `sortType=PRICE&sortDirection=ASC` gives you the 200 cheapest in
order.

parameters.name: priceType
parameters.description:
**What `minPrice` and `maxPrice` mean.** Optional; case-insensitive; defaults to
`DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`.

- `DAILY_WITH_EST_TOTAL`  -  the band is a **daily rate** (default). Verified: `50` - `100`
  returned cars priced `50.42` - `99.02` per day
- `TOTAL`  -  the band is the **whole-trip total** for the window in `startDateTime` /
  `endDateTime`, which is the number a guest actually pays. Only meaningful with dates: with
  no trip window there is no total to compare against
- `MONTHLY`  -  the band is a monthly figure for longer rentals. Send the real trip dates so
  the results are priced for the stay you are comparing

Ignored unless at least one of `minPrice` / `maxPrice` is sent.

**The two are not interchangeable.** A four-day trip under a `100` daily cap can total 400
plus fees, so a customer shopping to a trip budget wants `TOTAL`, and a customer comparing
cars wants the daily rate. For the exact itemisation of one car  -  daily rate, trip fee,
taxes, young-driver fee  -  call `/trip-quote`.

parameters.name: unlimitedMileageOnly
parameters.description:
**Only cars with unlimited miles included.** Optional; no mileage filter when omitted.

Most Turo listings include a daily mileage allowance and charge per mile beyond it. Set this
to `true` to keep only the listings with no cap at all  -  the ones to book for a road trip,
where an overage charge is the difference between a good price and a bad one.

Measured: `unlimitedMileageOnly=true` → 470 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline. It is a harsh
filter, and that is the real shape of the market rather than an artefact.

**There is deliberately no "maximum mileage" or "at least N miles" parameter.** Turo does
not expose a limited-mileage threshold because its behavior is not established. Each result
carries its own mileage allowance, so an "at least
200 miles a day" rule can be applied to the rows on the way out.

parameters.name: minFuelEconomy
parameters.description:
**Minimum fuel economy**, in miles per gallon. Optional; no economy floor when omitted.

A floor. Measured: `minFuelEconomy=35` → 1,151 of the 8,422 Los Angeles baseline.

`/search-filters` publishes the tiers the Turo app itself offers for the market you are
searching (`fuelEfficiencyProperties.options`, e.g. "25+ MPG  -  Good"), which are a good guide
to values that split the market usefully.

 **An economy bound of ANY value drops every listing that carries no economy figure, and
that is most of the electric market.** Measured: the 8,410-car Los Angeles baseline falls to
**7,013** under `minFuelEconomy=0`, so a floor of zero  -  which reads like "no filter at all"  - 
already removes 1,397 cars. Cross-checked against the engine filter: `engines=ELECTRIC` alone
is 992 cars, but `minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is **1**. A couple of hundred petrol
listings have no figure either (`engines=GAS` 6,185 → 5,976 with a zero floor). So an economy
bound is a petrol/diesel/hybrid question  -  use `engines=ELECTRIC` for the electric market
instead, and never send a `0` bound as a no-op.

Pair it with `maxFuelEconomy` for a band. A single car's city, highway and combined figures,
and its battery range, are on `/vehicle-features`.

parameters.name: maxFuelEconomy
parameters.description:
**Maximum fuel economy**, in miles per gallon. Optional; no economy ceiling when omitted.

A ceiling  -  the mirror of `minFuelEconomy`. Measured against the 8,410-car Los Angeles
baseline: `maxFuelEconomy=24` → **2,208**, `maxFuelEconomy=15` → **79**, and
`maxFuelEconomy=200` (the ceiling this parameter accepts) → **7,013**, which is every listing
that carries an economy figure at all  -  the same count a `minFuelEconomy=0` floor returns.
`maxFuelEconomy=0` → **0**.

Either bound works alone, and they combine into a band: `minFuelEconomy=16&maxFuelEconomy=24`
→ **2,111**, against **4,604** for `minFuelEconomy=25` on its own. The bands are disjoint, so
the bound genuinely partitions the market rather than overlapping slices of it.

**Two things it is actually for.** First, finding the thirsty end of the market  -  the V8s and
the big trucks, which no other filter isolates. Second, **walking past the 200-car response
cap**: split the economy range into disjoint bands (`0` - `15`, `16` - `24`, `25` - `200`) and
search each, exactly the way `minPrice`/`maxPrice` bands are used for the same purpose. The
bands do not overlap, so the results add up rather than repeating.

 **Same caveat as `minFuelEconomy`: any economy bound drops every listing with no economy
figure**, which is nearly the whole electric market  -  `engines=ELECTRIC` is 992 cars, but
`minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is 1. Read that parameter's note before banding.

`maxFuelEconomy=200` (the ceiling this parameter accepts) → **7,013**, which is every listing
that carries an economy figure at all  -  the same count a `minFuelEconomy=0` floor returns.
`maxFuelEconomy=0` → **0**.

Either bound works alone, and they combine into a band: `minFuelEconomy=16&maxFuelEconomy=24`
→ **2,111**, against **4,604** for `minFuelEconomy=25` on its own. The bands are disjoint, so
the bound genuinely partitions the market rather than overlapping slices of it.

**Two things it is actually for.** First, finding the thirsty end of the market  -  the V8s and
the big trucks, which no other filter isolates. Second, **walking past the 200-car response
cap**: split the economy range into disjoint bands (`0` - `15`, `16` - `24`, `25` - `200`) and
search each, exactly the way `minPrice`/`maxPrice` bands are used for the same purpose. The
bands do not overlap, so the results add up rather than repeating.

 **Same caveat as `minFuelEconomy`: any economy bound drops every listing with no economy
figure**, which is nearly the whole electric market  -  `engines=ELECTRIC` is 992 cars, but
`minFuelEconomy=0&engines=ELECTRIC` is 1. Read that parameter's note before banding.

parameters.name: sortType
parameters.description:
**Result ordering.** Optional and case-insensitive; Turo's own relevance ranking is used when
omitted.

- `RELEVANCE`  -  Turo's blended ranking of price, rating, distance and popularity. This is
  what the app shows
- `PRICE`  -  by price. **The single most useful ordering on this API**, because a response is
  capped at 200 cars: `sortDirection=ASC` gives you the cheapest 200 of the match set and
  `DESC` the most expensive 200 of the same set. Verified in Los Angeles: `ASC` returned
  `18.02` - `33.05` a day, `DESC` returned `208.65` - `2956.50`
- `DISTANCE`  -  nearest first, measured from the point you searched. Only meaningful for a
  point or `locationId` search; every result carries its own `location.distance`
- `SCORE`  -  Turo's quality score, highest first
- `RANDOMIZED`  -  deliberately shuffled. Useful for sampling a market, useless for anything
  you intend to repeat

Anything else is rejected with a `400`. `/search-filters` publishes the orderings the app
offers for a market, with their labels.

**Sorting never returns more cars  -  it returns different ones.** The cap is 200 either way;
the ordering decides which 200 of the `totalHits` matches you see.

**Repeatability, measured.** Two identical `RELEVANCE` searches returned the same 200 cars in
the same order, so the default view is stable enough to diff between runs. `PRICE` returns the
same 200 cars but re-orders cars that share a price between calls  -  the membership is stable,
the order within a tie is not, so compare sets rather than positions.

parameters.name: sortDirection
parameters.description:
**Which way to sort.** Optional; `ASC` (ascending) or `DESC` (descending); case-insensitive.

Only meaningful alongside `sortType`. With `sortType=PRICE`: `ASC` is cheapest-first and
`DESC` is most-expensive-first  -  verified as `18.02` - `33.05` and `208.65` - `2956.50` a day on
the same Los Angeles search.

**Run both directions to read both ends of a market in two calls.** Because each response is
capped at 200 cars, one `PRICE ASC` call plus one `PRICE DESC` call gives you the budget end
and the luxury end of the same match set, with `totalHits` telling you how big the middle
you did not see is.
